source.author: verg
source.text: Sternitur infelix alieno volnere caelumque aspicit et dulcis moriens reminiscitur Argos tum pius Aeneas hastam iacit: illa per orbem aere cavum triplici, per linea terga tribusque transit intextum tauris opus imaque sedit inguine, sed viris haud pertulit.
source.text_original: Sternitur infelix alieno volnere caelumque / aspicit et dulcis moriens reminiscitur Argos / tum pius Aeneas hastam iacit: illa per orbem / aere cavum triplici, per linea terga tribusque / transit intextum tauris opus imaque sedit / inguine, sed viris haud pertulit.
source.text_english: The unhappy man is laid low by another’s wound and looks up at the sky, and as he dies he recalls dear Argos. Then dutiful Aeneas throws his spear: it passed through the hollow shield of bronze in a triple circle, through the linen backing, through the woven work of three bulls, and sank into the lowest groin, but it did not reach the man.

reuse.author: val
reuse.text: proximus hinc Butes Actaeis dives ab oris; innumeras nam claudit apes longaque superbus fuscat nube diem, dum plenas nectare cellas pandit et in dulcem reges dimittit Hymetton.
reuse.text_original: proximus hinc Butes Actaeis dives ab oris; / innumeras nam claudit apes longaque superbus / fuscat nube diem, dum plenas nectare cellas / pandit et in dulcem reges dimittit Hymetton.
reuse.text_english: Next from here was Butes, rich from the Actaean shores; for he keeps innumerable bees shut up and, proud, darkens the day with a long cloud, as he opens the cells full of nectar and sends the kings out into sweet Hymettus.
